record.original_question: Let A be an Artin local ring over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0, finite-dimensional over k as a vector space. If l denotes module length and Ω_A^1 is the module of Kähler differentials of A, is it always true that l(Ω_A^1) >= l(A) - 1, with equality if and only if A is isomorphic to k[x]/(x^n)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, and let $A$ be an Artinian local $k$-algebra that is finite-dimensional as a $k$-vector space. Denote by $\ell(M)$ the length of an $A$-module $M$, and by $\Omega_{A/k}^1$ the module of Kähler differentials of $A$ over $k$.

Decide whether the following statement holds: 
$$\ell(\Omega_{A/k}^1) \;\geq\; \ell(A)-1,$$
with equality if and only if $A$ is isomorphic (as a $k$-algebra) to $k[x]/(x^n)$ for some integer $n\geq 1$.
artifact.category_tag: Kähler differentials of Artin local rings
artifact.status_search_result: This is closely related to (an Artinian formulation of) Berger's conjecture. Cortiñas–Geller–Weibel introduced "the Artinian Berger conjecture" in 1995, and subsequent work (e.g., Hübl, and more recent papers up to 2022–2023 on Berger's conjecture) has established the statement in numerous cases, but a fully general proof for arbitrary finite-dimensional Artin local k-algebras in characteristic 0 does not appear to be in the literature. The problem appears to remain open in full generality.

status_evidence.title: The Artinian Berger Conjecture
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes an Artinian version of Berger's Conjecture for curves, concerning the module of Kähler differentials of an algebra.
status_evidence.claim: The question is essentially the Artinian Berger conjecture, formulated and partially settled in 1995.

status_evidence.title: Torsion in Differentials and Berger's Conjecture
status_evidence.snippet: New cases of Berger's conjecture obtained by extending works of Güttes and Cortiñas et al.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work continues to establish further cases, indicating the conjecture is not yet settled in full generality.
